newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin stable but political future questioned.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin stable but political future questioned.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's condition was described as more stable on Saturday as he fought a bout of pneumonia, but a liberal newspaper raised the question of whether it was time for him to step aside.

The Kremlin said doctors had examined the 65-year-old president at Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital where he was taken on Wednesday evening with pneumonia, just two months after a multiple heart bypass operation.

"In their opinion, the patient's condition has stabilised, his activity has grown somewhat," a brief Kremlin statement said. Yeltsin's temperature was normal and his blood pressure stable. The next health bulletin was due on Sunday.
Some Russian commentators now suggest the president, who has been largely absent from the public view since his re-election in July, should consider resigning.
"Regretfully, it is obvious that the president has no strength left to attend to affairs of the state properly," the liberal Komsomolskaya Pravda newspaper said on Saturday.
The Russian constitution concentrates political power in the hands of the president, and during his absence many pressing issues have gone unresolved.

"Power in Russia is organised in such a way that everything is stuck without approval from the very top, be it a president or a general secretary (of the Soviet Communist Party)," Komsomolskaya Pravda said.
Other newspaper have expressed doubts about the president's ability to rule the huge country and solve its many problems.
Top Kremlin doctor, Sergei Mironov, said on Friday Yeltsin would have to stay at least another three days in hospital and would need a three-week rest before returning to work.
He made clear Yeltsin was frustrated by his new illness, which has prevented him fully re-asserting his power.

"Of course I cannot say Boris Nikolayevich feels comfortable spiritually," Mironov told reporters. "Of course this is depressing him, of course his mood is not a very happy one but I see no reason for particular pessimism."

Mironov ruled out any direct link between pneumonia and the heart surgery Yeltsin underwent on November 5. That view has been endorsed by veteran U.S. cardiologist Michael DeBakey, who advised the Russian doctors who conducted the operation.
But he added that Yeltsin had been weakened by the surgery and should have been admitted to hospital earlier.
Some opposition political figures were quick to declare that Yeltsin was no longer able to rule Russia.
Presidential hopeful Alexander Lebed, sacked by Yeltsin as security adviser last October for being overtly ambitious, said on Friday that the illness had left the country adrift.
Lebed said his new medical setback was a tragedy for the whole country. "A power vacuum has been created," he said.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, constitutionally number two, was on holiday near Moscow.
Commercial NTV television said the president's chief-of- staff Anatoly Chubais, reviled by Lebed as a 'regent' wielding vast power, had cancelled a trip to the United States.
Some politicians, uneasy over Yeltsin's long absence, have called for changes in the constitution to give more authority to parliament and reduce the president's vast powers.
